title: Water Cycle Travel Station
subtitle: How does one drop of water travel around Earth?
coreQuestion: How does water rise from the sea, become rain, and return to the ground?
learningGoals: Know the water cycle includes evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.
Understand that the Sun helps water become vapor.
Connect clouds, rain, rivers, and oceans in one cycle.
misconceptions: Rain happens because clouds leak like bags of water.
Water disappears after it is used.

hero.title: Water Cycle Travel Station
hero.lead: A drop of water can rise from the sea, become a cloud, fall as rain, and return to the ground.
hero.sceneExplanation: The main scene is a circular droplet path: sunlight warms the ocean, vapor rises, clouds form, rain falls on mountains and plants, and water flows through rivers back to the sea.
hero.childPrompt: Start at the ocean and help one water drop find its way home.
hero.parentPrompt: Focus on cycle and state change before introducing technical weather terms.

classificationGroups.name: Places water stays
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Water can be in oceans, rivers, soil, and plants.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Build a spatial sense of where water appears.
classificationGroups.misconception: Water only exists in cups or taps.

classificationGroups.name: Changes in the sky
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Water vapor rises, gathers as clouds, and falls as rain.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Use child-friendly words for evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.
classificationGroups.misconception: Clouds are cotton and rain means clouds break.

classificationGroups.name: What powers the trip
classificationGroups.childExplanation: The Sun warms water and helps it become vapor.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Do not explain thermodynamics; just highlight solar energy.
classificationGroups.misconception: Water suddenly flies into the sky by itself.

classificationGroups.name: The way back down
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Rain flows into streams, rivers, and oceans.
classificationGroups.misconception: Rainwater stops being part of the cycle after it falls.

representativeObjects.name: Sun
representativeObjects.childExplanation: The Sun warms water on land and sea, turning some of it into vapor.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking the water cycle does not need the Sun.

representativeObjects.name: Ocean
representativeObjects.childExplanation: The ocean holds a lot of water and is an important starting point.

representativeObjects.name: Water vapor
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Water vapor is light and often invisible, so it can rise into the air.

representativeObjects.name: Cloud
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A cloud contains many tiny water droplets or ice crystals.

representativeObjects.name: Rain
representativeObjects.childExplanation: When droplets grow bigger and heavier, they fall as rain.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking rain means the cloud breaks apart.

representativeObjects.name: River
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Rainwater can gather into streams and rivers.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking river water never returns to the sea.

representativeObjects.name: Plant
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Plants take in water and can also send some vapor back into the air.

steps.childExplanation: The Sun warms water on the ocean and land, and some water becomes vapor.
steps.parentNote: This is evaporation in child-friendly language.

steps.childExplanation: Light water vapor rises into the sky with the air.
When vapor meets cooler air, many tiny droplets gather to form clouds.
When droplets grow bigger and heavier, they fall back as rain.
steps.parentNote: Rain, snow, and hail can be introduced later.

steps.childExplanation: Rain enters soil, streams, rivers, and eventually many drops return to the sea.
steps.parentNote: Emphasize a loop rather than a straight line.

secondaryMechanism.title: Plants also join the water cycle

steps.childExplanation: Plant roots take water from the soil.
steps.parentNote: Connect to watering plants at home.

steps.childExplanation: Leaves can send some water vapor back into the air.
Places with more plants often feel cooler and more humid.

comparePairs.title: Cloud vs Cotton

a.name: Cloud
points: made of tiny droplets or ice crystals

b.name: Cotton
points: can be held in your hand

comparePairs.childConclusion: Clouds look soft, but they are not cotton.

comparePairs.title: Evaporation vs Boiling

a.name: Evaporation
points: can happen on oceans and ground

comparePairs.childConclusion: Ocean water can evaporate without boiling.

comparePairs.title: River vs Ocean

a.name: River
points: carries water toward lakes or seas

comparePairs.childConclusion: Rivers and oceans are connected in the same cycle.

clickTasks.title: What are clouds mostly made of?

speakTemplates: Water changes from ____ into ____ and rises into the sky.
After rain falls, water can flow into _____.
The water cycle is not a straight line; it is a _____.
parentTips: Use a foggy mirror, droplets on a cold cup, or water under a pot lid to explain state change.
Do not force terminology first; let the child tell the story of the cycle.
Ask the child to draw arrows connecting Sun, ocean, cloud, rain, and river.

intro: The Sun, ocean, clouds, rain, rivers, and plants all join the journey.
keyFacts: The Sun helps water turn into invisible vapor.
Water vapor gathers in the sky to form clouds.
Rain returns to the ground, rivers, oceans, and plants.
copy.explainPrompt: Can you follow one drop of water from the ocean to the sky and back again?

acceptanceCriteria: The child can name at least three water-cycle steps.
The child knows the Sun helps water evaporate.
The child can use arrows to show water returning to rivers or the ocean.
